title: 27 — Design a Digital Wallet
html:
27 — Design a Digital Wallet

The one idea: a balance transfer must debit one account and credit another atomically, but at 1M TPS the accounts live on different shards. The options are distributed transactions (2PC, TC/C, sagas) or event sourcing: an ordered log of validated commands and events per account from which balances are derived — reproducible, auditable, and fast with in-memory state and snapshots.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Balance transfer between two wallets of the same platform.
  • 1,000,000 TPS; reliability ≥ 99.99%; transactional guarantees; reproducibility (reconstruct any historical balance by replaying data); auditing.

Estimates: each transfer = 2 operations (debit + credit) → 2M ops/s. If one DB node handles ~1,000 TPS (typical for a relational node doing transactions), that's ~2,000 nodes — the design must scale out.

Step 2 — High-level design

Approach 1: in-memory sharding (Redis)

account_id → balance in Redis, sharded by account via a partition map in ZooKeeper; a wallet service does balance[A] -= 1; balance[C] += 1.

❌ Two separate updates on two nodes are not atomic — a crash between them loses or creates money. Also not durable.

Approach 2: distributed transactions on relational shards

2PC (two-phase commit): a coordinator asks all shards to prepare (lock rows), then commit. Correct, but blocking — coordinator failure holds locks; slow.

TC/C (Try–Confirm/Cancel): two independent local transactions per phase at the business level:

Phase Account A Account C
Try Debit $1 (balance − 1) No-op
Confirm No-op Credit $1
Cancel (if try fails) Refund $1 No-op

Needs a phase status table (per distributed transaction) stored with the initiating shard, and must handle out-of-order execution (cancel arriving before try).

Saga: a linear sequence of local transactions with compensating transactions on failure; orchestrated (central coordinator ✅) or choreographed (events).

TC/C Saga
Compensation In Cancel phase In rollback phase
Execution Any order Linear
Parallelism Yes Sequential (orchestrated)
Fits Latency-sensitive, many parties Microservices, few steps

These give atomicity, but not reproducibility — we can't prove how a balance got its value if an update was wrong.

Step 3 — Deep dive: event sourcing

3.1 Terms

Term Meaning Example
Command Intent from outside, may be invalid "Transfer $1 from A to C"
Event Validated fact, immutable, past tense "A debited $1", "C credited $1"
State Derived from applying events balance[A] = 4
State machine Validates commands → emits events; applies events → updates state Wallet service

Commands are stored in order (a queue/log); the state machine processes them sequentially, validates (sufficient funds?), emits events, and applies events to state. Events are deterministic — replaying them always gives the same state → reproducibility and audit.

---
title: Event sourcing — command, event and state
---
flowchart LR
    Cmd["Command log<br/>(Kafka / local file)"] --> SM["State machine<br/>validate → emit"]
    SM --> Ev["Event log"]
    Ev --> SM2["Apply events"]
    SM2 --> St[("State<br/>balances")]
    St -. read .-> SM
    Ev --> Snap[("Snapshots<br/>periodic")]

3.2 Making it fast

  • File-based command/event logs on local disk (append-only, sequential writes, mmap) instead of Kafka round-trips.
  • State in RocksDB/SQLite locally or fully in memory.
  • Snapshots of state periodically → replay only from the last snapshot.

3.3 Reliability

Local disk on one node is a SPOF → replicate the event log with Raft: a leader accepts commands and replicates events to followers; a follower takes over on leader failure. Only the event list needs replicating — state and snapshots can be rebuilt from it.

3.4 CQRS

Clients read balances from read-only state machines that consume the event stream (possibly lagging slightly) — writes and reads scale independently. The response to a write can be pushed back when the event is applied.

3.5 Distributed event sourcing

One Raft group handles a partition of accounts. A transfer across partitions → saga or TC/C across Raft groups, each step an event-sourced local transaction. You get all three: scale (partitions), atomicity (saga/TC/C), reproducibility (event sourcing).

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Walk the progression: Redis (fast, not atomic) → distributed transactions (atomic, not reproducible) → event sourcing + Raft + CQRS + sagas (fast, atomic, reproducible, auditable).

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Event store: EventStoreDB, Marten (event sourcing on PostgreSQL), or a SQL Events table (StreamId, Version with unique constraint for optimistic concurrency, Type, Data, Timestamp).
  • Cosmos DB as event store: partition by accountId, transactional batch within a partition, change feed to drive projections (CQRS read models).
  • Sagas: MassTransit state machines, NServiceBus sagas, or Durable Functions orchestrations with compensation steps.
  • Single-writer per account: Orleans grains (one grain per wallet serialises commands naturally, with journaled/event-sourced grain storage).
  • Money arithmetic: decimal; never double.

Review checklist

  • Estimate → thousands of nodes → sharding is forced.
  • Why independent updates on two shards are unsafe.
  • 2PC vs TC/C vs saga, with failure behaviour.
  • Event sourcing: command → event → state; determinism → reproducibility.
  • Snapshots, local logs, Raft replication, CQRS reads.
